content: A Limited Symptom Attack (LSA), also known as a Limited Symptom Panic Attack (LPA), is a less severe form of a panic attack. It is characterized by the presence of fewer than four symptoms typically associated with a full-blown panic attack, as defined by the American Psychiatric Association in 1994. For instance, an individual may experience a sudden onset of intense dizziness or trembling, accompanied by a fear that something catastrophic is about to occur. Individuals with panic disorder often experience a combination of both full-blown panic attacks and LSAs. LSAs are commonly observed in conditions such as anxiety disorders, specific phobias, panic disorder, and agoraphobia. However, experiencing an LSA does not necessarily indicate the presence of a mental illness. It is not uncommon for individuals recovering from or undergoing treatment for panic attacks and panic disorder to experience LSAs. According to the DSM-IV, during an LSA, fewer than four of the following symptoms are experienced, in contrast to a full-blown panic attack, which requires the presence of four or more symptoms: Shortness of breath (dyspnea) Heart palpitations Trembling or shaking Dizziness Chest pain or discomfort Excessive sweating (perspiration) Hot flashes Headache Feelings of unreality (derealization) Tingling or numbness (paresthesia) Hyperventilation Nausea Vertigo Lightheadedness Burning sensations Sensation of choking Fear of dying Fear of losing control or going insane The duration of an LSA is similar to that of a full-blown panic attack, typically peaking within 10 minutes. However, LSAs can be as brief as 1 to 5 minutes or may occur as a series of episodes that fluctuate in intensity over a period of several hours.
